content: This House Would Place Development of Advanced Autonomous AI Under International Licensing Oversight. Frontier AI systems present systemic, irreversible catastrophic risks comparable to nuclear energy or synthetic biotechnology. Independent corporate actors lack the economic incentives to prioritize global safety over race dynamics. International licensing establishes mandatory safety audits, alignment verification, and containment tripwires. State-managed international licensing cartels stifle technological innovation, entrench corporate incumbents through regulatory capture, and drive development into clandestine black markets. Open decentralized research is the single most effective vector for democratizing AI defensive security.

content: This House Would Institute an Unconditional Universal Basic Income Financed by Automation Taxes. As robotics and generative AI decouple labor from production, structural technological unemployment will dismantle consumer demand. Universal Basic Income restores economic agency, eradicates absolute poverty, and decouples human survival from obsolete industrial wage labor. Taxing automation imposes an inefficient capital penalty on technological productivity. UBI triggers demand-side inflation without expanding productive capacity, severely reduces labor force participation, and strains sovereign fiscal solvency.

content: This House Would Legally Ban All Post-Employment Non-Compete Clauses in High-Technology Sectors. Non-compete clauses suppress labor mobility, depress wage growth, and trap innovation within stagnant legacy firms. California's historic ban on non-competes was the singular catalyst that powered Silicon Valley's entrepreneurial explosion through cross-pollination of talent. Without reasonable non-compete protections, high-technology firms cannot justify massive multi-year capital investments into trade secrets and R&D. Competitors can poach key architects solely to expropriate proprietary intellectual capital without compensation.

content: Resolved: The development of autonomous weapons systems should be prohibited by international treaty. Autonomous weapons remove human moral accountability from lethal force decisions, lower the geopolitical threshold for entering armed conflict, and risk catastrophic algorithmic escalation. The affirmative delegate assumes human decision-making in high-stress combat is inherently moral and reliable. Empirical history shows human soldiers panic, commit atrocities, and misidentify targets under fear. Autonomous targeting systems operate on precise optical sensors, adhere strictly to international humanitarian law algorithms, and reduce civilian collateral damage by eliminating human panic. Furthermore, treaties cannot be verified against rogue state adversaries, leaving peaceful democracies defenseless against unconstrained automated threats.
